items.subject: Physics
items.question: What is the primary difference between static friction and kinetic friction in terms of when they occur?
items.answer_guide: Static friction opposes the tendency of motion (stationary), while kinetic friction acts when surfaces are sliding.
items.explanation: Static friction prevents motion; kinetic friction opposes existing relative motion.

items.subject: Physics
items.question: A 5 kg box is on a level floor with μ_s = 0.6 and g = 10 m/s^2. Will the box move if a horizontal force of 20 N is applied?
items.answer_guide: N = 50 N; f_s_max = 0.6 * 50 = 30 N. Since 20 N < 30 N, the box will not move.
items.explanation: Compare the applied force to the maximum static friction.

items.subject: Physics
items.question: A block is held stationary on a surface by a horizontal force F. If the coefficient of static friction is μ_s, what happens to the friction force if F is doubled, provided the block remains stationary?
items.answer_guide: The friction force also doubles.
items.explanation: Static friction adjusts its value to balance the applied force up to its maximum limit.

items.subject: Physics
items.question: How does the gravitational force between two masses change if the distance between their centers is doubled?
items.answer_guide: The force becomes one fourth (1/4) of the original force.
items.explanation: Gravitational force follows an inverse-square law (F ∝ 1/r²).

items.subject: Physics
items.question: Two spheres of mass m1 and m2 are separated by distance r. If m1 is doubled and r is halved, what is the new force in terms of the original force F?
items.explanation: Apply the formula F = Gm1m2/r^2 with the new values.

items.subject: Physics
items.question: Why can the gravitational field of a spherical body be treated as if all its mass were concentrated at its center for points outside the sphere?
items.answer_guide: Because the field behaves as if the mass were concentrated at the center for any external point.
items.explanation: This is a property of spherical symmetry in gravitation.

items.subject: Physics
items.question: What is the relationship between impulse and the change in momentum of an object?
items.answer_guide: Impulse is equal to the change in momentum of the object.
items.explanation: Fundamental definition of the impulse-momentum theorem.

items.subject: Physics
items.question: A 0.5 kg ball moving at 8 m/s is caught and brought to rest. Calculate the impulse delivered to the ball.
items.answer_guide: Δp = m(v_final - v_initial) = 0.5(0 - 8) = -4 kg m/s. Impulse = -4 N s.
items.explanation: Impulse equals the change in momentum (final minus initial).

items.subject: Physics
items.question: Two objects of different masses are subjected to the same impulse. Which one will experience a greater change in velocity, and why?
items.answer_guide: The object with the smaller mass will experience a greater change in velocity because Δv = Impulse/m.
items.explanation: Analyzes the inverse relationship between mass and velocity change for a constant impulse.

items.subject: Physics
items.question: What is the purpose of using significant figures when reporting a measured value?
items.answer_guide: To communicate the precision appropriate to the instrument used for measurement.
items.explanation: Significant figures indicate the reliability of the reported digits.

items.subject: Physics
items.question: A student records a length as 5.4 cm using a ruler with a resolution of 0.1 cm. Is reporting the value as 5.400 cm correct? Why?
items.answer_guide: No, it is incorrect.
items.explanation: Reporting 5.400 cm implies unsupported precision beyond the instrument's 0.1 cm resolution.

items.subject: Physics
items.question: When calculating the area of a rectangle from two independent measurements of length and width, how is the uncertainty of the result determined?
items.answer_guide: Uncertainty propagation follows the mathematical operation (multiplication) used to calculate the result.
items.explanation: For products, relative uncertainties are typically combined to find the total uncertainty.

items.subject: Physics
items.chapter: System of Particles and Rotational Motion
items.question: What does the moment of inertia of a body represent in rotational motion?
items.answer_guide: It measures the body's resistance to angular acceleration about a chosen axis.
items.explanation: Conceptual definition of moment of inertia.

items.subject: Physics
items.chapter: System of Particles and Rotational Motion
items.question: Calculate the moment of inertia of a system consisting of two point masses of 0.5 kg each, located 0.2 m from the axis of rotation.
items.explanation: Direct application of the point mass formula for moment of inertia.

items.subject: Physics
items.chapter: System of Particles and Rotational Motion
items.question: If the axis of rotation for a rigid body is shifted to a position further from the mass distribution, how does the angular acceleration change for a constant applied torque?
items.answer_guide: Shifting the axis increases r, which increases I (Σmr²). Since α = τ/I, for a constant τ, the angular acceleration α will decrease.
items.explanation: Analyzes the relationship between axis position, moment of inertia, and angular acceleration.

items.subject: Physics
items.question: According to Newton's second law, in which direction does the acceleration of an object point relative to the net force acting on it?
items.answer_guide: The acceleration points in the same direction as the net force.
items.explanation: Newton's second law states F_net = ma, where acceleration is proportional to and in the direction of the net force.

items.subject: Physics
items.question: A 5 kg object changes its velocity from 2 m/s to 8 m/s in 2 seconds. Calculate the net force acting on the object.
items.explanation: Apply F = ma using the change in velocity over time to find acceleration.

items.subject: Physics
items.question: Two forces act on a 3 kg mass: 10 N to the right and 4 N to the left. If the mass starts from rest, what is its velocity after 4 seconds?
items.explanation: Forces must be added as vectors to find the net force before calculating acceleration and final velocity.

items.subject: Physics
items.question: In ideal projectile motion neglecting air resistance, what is the horizontal acceleration of the projectile?
items.answer_guide: The horizontal acceleration is zero.
items.explanation: Without air resistance, there are no horizontal forces acting on the projectile.

items.subject: Physics
items.question: A ball is launched horizontally at 15 m/s from a height of 45 m. Using g = 10 m/s^2, calculate the horizontal range.
items.explanation: Use the vertical fall time to determine the distance traveled horizontally.

items.subject: Physics
items.question: A projectile is launched horizontally from a ledge. If the launch height is quadrupled while the initial horizontal velocity remains constant, how does the horizontal range change?
items.answer_guide: The range doubles.
items.explanation: Time t is proportional to sqrt(h). If h becomes 4h, t becomes 2t. Since range = v*t, range also doubles.

items.subject: Physics
items.question: In simple harmonic motion, what is the relationship between acceleration and displacement from the equilibrium position?
items.answer_guide: Acceleration is proportional to displacement and points in the opposite direction (a = -ω²x).
items.explanation: This defining characteristic ensures the object is always pulled back toward equilibrium.

items.subject: Physics
items.question: An object in SHM has a position given by x(t) = 0.1 cos(2t) meters. Determine the amplitude and the period.
items.answer_guide: Amplitude = 0.1 m; Period T = 2π/ω = 2π/2 = π s.
items.explanation: Identify amplitude from the coefficient and period from the angular frequency ω=2.

items.subject: Physics
items.question: If the angular frequency ω of a system in SHM is doubled, how does the period T of the oscillation change?
items.answer_guide: The period is halved.
items.explanation: Since T = 2π/ω, the period is inversely proportional to the angular frequency.

items.subject: Physics
items.question: In a standing wave, what is the difference between a node and an antinode?
items.answer_guide: A node is a point of permanent zero displacement; an antinode is a point of maximum oscillation.
items.explanation: Basic definitions of standing wave characteristics.

items.subject: Physics
items.question: In a standing wave pattern on a string, the distance between two consecutive nodes is 0.3 m. What is the wavelength of the wave?
items.answer_guide: Distance between adjacent nodes = λ/2. Therefore, λ = 2 * 0.3 = 0.6 m.
items.explanation: Application of the relationship between node spacing and wavelength.

items.subject: Physics
items.question: Two waves of the same frequency and amplitude travel in opposite directions on a string. Describe the resulting displacement at a point where the waves interfere destructively at all times.
items.answer_guide: The displacement is always zero. This point is called a node, formed by the algebraic sum of opposite displacements.
items.explanation: Analyzes the superposition principle leading to the formation of a node.

items.subject: Physics
items.question: Why do most materials expand when they are heated?
items.answer_guide: They expand because the average separation between their particles increases.
items.explanation: Microscopic explanation of thermal expansion.

items.subject: Physics
items.question: A steel rod of length 1.5 m has a coefficient of linear expansion α = 1.2×10⁻⁵ K⁻¹. Calculate the change in length if the temperature increases by 100 K.
items.explanation: Direct application of the linear expansion formula.

items.subject: Physics
items.question: Two rods of the same initial length but different materials (α₁ > α₂) are heated by the same temperature ΔT. Compare their final lengths and explain the result.
items.answer_guide: The rod with α₁ will be longer. Since ΔL = αL₀ΔT, a larger α results in a greater increase in length for the same L₀ and ΔT.
items.explanation: Analyzes the effect of the expansion coefficient on final length.

items.subject: Physics
items.chapter: System of Particles and Rotational Motion
items.question: What are the two conditions required for a rigid body to be in static equilibrium?
items.answer_guide: The net external force must be zero and the net external torque must be zero.
items.explanation: Definition of static equilibrium for a rigid body.

items.subject: Physics
items.chapter: System of Particles and Rotational Motion
items.question: A force of 15 N is applied perpendicular to a wrench at a distance of 0.25 m from the bolt. Calculate the magnitude of the torque.
items.explanation: Direct application of the torque formula for a perpendicular force.

items.subject: Physics
items.chapter: System of Particles and Rotational Motion
items.question: A 2 m long uniform beam is balanced at its center. If a 10 N force is applied 0.5 m to the left of the center, where must a 5 N force be applied to maintain equilibrium?
items.answer_guide: Left torque = 10 * 0.5 = 5 N m. Right torque must be 5 N m. 5 * r = 5, so r = 1.0 m to the right of the center.
items.explanation: Uses the principle that net torque must be zero for equilibrium.

items.subject: Physics
items.question: If a vector A makes an angle θ with the positive x-axis, what are the formulas for its x and y components?
items.answer_guide: Ax = A cosθ and Ay = A sinθ.
items.explanation: Standard trigonometric resolution of a vector into perpendicular components.

items.subject: Physics
items.question: A force of 20 N is applied at an angle of 60° above the positive x-axis. Calculate the horizontal and vertical components.
items.explanation: Direct application of component formulas with given magnitude and angle.

items.subject: Physics
items.question: A vector has components Ax = 3 units and Ay = -4 units. Determine the magnitude of the vector and the angle it makes with the positive x-axis.
items.answer_guide: Magnitude A = sqrt(3² + (-4)²) = 5 units. Angle θ = tan⁻¹(-4/3) ≈ -53.1°.
items.explanation: Inverse process of resolution using Pythagorean theorem and tangent function.

items.subject: Physics
items.question: Define average velocity and state whether it is a scalar or vector quantity.
items.answer_guide: Average velocity is the total displacement divided by the elapsed time. It is a vector quantity.
items.explanation: Based on the definition of average velocity as displacement over time.

items.subject: Physics
items.question: A cyclist travels 3 km East and then 4 km West in a total time of 2 hours. Calculate the average velocity.
items.answer_guide: Displacement = 3 - 4 = -1 km (or 1 km West). Average velocity = -1 km / 2 h = -0.5 km/h (or 0.5 km/h West).
items.explanation: Average velocity depends on net displacement, not total distance.

items.subject: Physics
items.question: A particle moves in a circular path of radius R. After completing exactly one full revolution in time T, compare its average speed and average velocity.
items.answer_guide: Average speed is (2πR)/T. Average velocity is 0 because the net displacement after one full revolution is zero.
items.explanation: Distinguishes between distance-based speed and displacement-based velocity.

items.subject: Physics
items.question: What is the relationship between the net work done on an object and its kinetic energy?
items.answer_guide: The net work done on an object equals its change in kinetic energy (W_net = ΔK).
items.explanation: This is the fundamental definition of the work-energy theorem.

items.subject: Physics
items.question: A 4 kg block increases its speed from 3 m/s to 5 m/s. Calculate the net work done on the block.
items.explanation: Calculate the change in kinetic energy using the given mass and velocities.

items.subject: Physics
items.question: A block is pushed across a floor by a force acting at a 90-degree angle to the displacement. If the block's speed remains constant, what is the net work done on the block?
items.answer_guide: The net work is 0 J.
items.explanation: A force perpendicular to displacement does no work, and constant speed implies ΔK = 0.
